question: In which year was the State Bank of India constituted, by the conversion of the Imperial Bank of India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1955.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The State Bank of India was constituted on 1 July 1955, under the State Bank of India Act, 1955, by taking over the Imperial Bank of India. (भारतीय स्टेट बैंक — 1955)

 

• The step followed the recommendation of the All India Rural Credit Survey Committee, chaired by A.D. Gorwala, which held that a state-partnered and state-sponsored bank was needed to extend banking to the countryside.

 

• The Imperial Bank of India had itself been formed in 1921 by the amalgamation of the three Presidency Banks — those of Bengal (1806), Bombay (1840) and Madras (1843).

 

• SBI is today India's largest public sector bank, with its headquarters at Mumbai.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Landmarks in the history of Indian banking:

 

• 1770 – Bank of Hindustan, the first bank in India

 

• 1806 – Bank of Bengal, the first Presidency Bank

 

• 1921 – Imperial Bank of India formed

 

• 1935 – Reserve Bank of India established, on the recommendation of the Hilton Young Commission

 

• 1955 – State Bank of India constituted

 

• 1969 – 14 major banks nationalised; 1980 – 6 more

 

NOTE

 

• 1949 (Option 2): The year of the Banking Regulation Act, and also the year the RBI was nationalised — a genuine banking landmark, and the strongest distractor here.

 

• 1959 (Option 3): The year of the State Bank of India (Subsidiary Banks) Act, under which the former banks of the princely states became SBI's associate banks. These were merged into SBI itself in 2017.

 

• 1969 (Option 4): The year in which 14 major commercial banks were nationalised under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.

question: In which year did Babur defeat Rana Sanga at the Battle of Khanwa?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1527.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Battle of Khanwa was fought on 16 March 1527, near Fatehpur Sikri, between Babur and Rana Sanga (Sangram Singh) of Mewar. (खानवा का युद्ध — 1527)

 

• Babur won, and the victory was in some ways more decisive than Panipat: at Panipat he had destroyed the Lodi Sultanate, but Khanwa broke the Rajput confederacy, which was the only remaining power capable of expelling him from northern India.

 

• Before the battle Babur declared it a jihad, took the title "Ghazi", and publicly renounced wine, breaking his gold and silver drinking vessels to steady the morale of his army.

 

• Babur again used the Tulughma (flanking) formation and the Araba (cart) defence with field artillery, as he had at Panipat.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Babur's four decisive battles:

 

• Panipat (First), 1526 – defeated Ibrahim Lodi; founded the Mughal empire

 

• Khanwa, 1527 – defeated Rana Sanga of Mewar

 

• Chanderi, 1528 – defeated Medini Rai

 

• Ghaghra, 1529 – defeated the Afghan confederacy in Bihar and Bengal

 

• Babur wrote his memoirs, the Baburnama (or *Tuzuk-i-Baburi*), in Chagatai Turkish. He died in 1530 at Agra and was later buried at Kabul.

 

NOTE

 

• 1526 (Option 1): The year of the First Battle of Panipat, in which Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi and founded the Mughal empire.

 

• 1529 (Option 3): The year of the Battle of Ghaghra, Babur's last major engagement, against the Afghans.

 

• 1530 (Option 4): The year of Babur's death, when he was succeeded by Humayun.

question: What was the name of Guru Gobind Singh before the founding of the Khalsa in 1699?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gobind Rai.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The tenth Guru was named Gobind Rai at birth, and took the name Gobind SINGH at the founding of the Khalsa on Baisakhi, 1699, at Anandpur Sahib. (गोबिंद राय — गुरु गोबिंद सिंह)

 

• At that ceremony he administered Amrit to the Panj Pyare (the five beloved ones), gave every male the surname Singh ("lion") and every female Kaur ("princess"), and then remarkably received Amrit from them in turn.

 

• He was born at Patna Sahib in 1666, and was the son of Guru Tegh Bahadur.

 

• Before his death in 1708 at Nanded, he ended the line of living Gurus and conferred the guruship upon the Guru Granth Sahib.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The birth names of the Gurus are a favourite in examinations:

 

• Guru Angad – born Lehna

 

• Guru Ram Das – born Bhai Jetha

 

• Guru Tegh Bahadur – born Tyag Mal; renamed for his bravery in battle

 

• Guru Gobind Singh – born Gobind Rai

 

• Guru Gobind Singh instituted the five Ks — *Kesh, Kangha, Kara, Kachera and Kirpan* — and composed the Dasam Granth and the Zafarnama, his letter to Aurangzeb.

 

NOTE

 

• Tyag Mal (Option 2): The birth name of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru and the father of Guru Gobind Singh. He was renamed *Tegh Bahadur*, "brave of the sword".

 

• Bhai Jetha (Option 3): The birth name of Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, who founded Amritsar.

 

• Lehna (Option 4): The birth name of Guru Angad Dev, the second Guru, who gave the Sikhs the Gurmukhi script.

question: The "Rolling Plan" was adopted in India in place of the Five Year Plan during the tenure of which government?
option_1: The Congress government under Indira Gandhi
option_2: The Congress government under Rajiv Gandhi
option_3: The Janata Party government under Morarji Desai
option_4: The National Front government under V.P. Singh
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Janata Party government under Morarji Desai.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Rolling Plan was adopted in 1978 by the Janata Party government headed by Morarji Desai. (रोलिंग प्लान — जनता पार्टी सरकार, 1978)

 

• On coming to power the Janata government terminated the Fifth Five Year Plan (1974-79) one year early, in 1978, and replaced fixed five-year planning with a rolling arrangement.

 

• In a Rolling Plan the targets and allocations are revised every year in the light of what has actually happened, and the plan is extended forward by a year each time — so that a plan of fixed length never comes to an end.

 

• The concept was introduced in India by the economist Gunnar Myrdal, and the plan itself was framed under Professor D.T. Lakdawala.

 

• The Rolling Plan was itself abandoned in 1980, when the Congress returned to power and launched the Sixth Five Year Plan (1980-85).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• There have thus been two breaks in India's five-year planning:

 

• 1966-69 — three Annual Plans, the "Plan Holiday", after the failure of the Third Plan

 

• 1978-80 — the Rolling Plan under the Janata government

 

• The advantage claimed for a rolling plan is flexibility; the objection to it is that constantly shifting targets make long-term commitment and evaluation difficult.

 

NOTE

 

• Indira Gandhi (Option 1): Under her the Fifth Plan was framed, with its slogan "Garibi Hatao" and the Minimum Needs Programme — the very plan the Janata government cut short.

 

• Rajiv Gandhi (Option 2): Prime Minister from 1984 to 1989, during the Seventh Plan (1985-90), which emphasised food, work and productivity.

 

• V.P. Singh (Option 4): Prime Minister 1989-90. The political instability of those years meant that two Annual Plans (1990-92) were framed before the Eighth Plan began — a third interruption, but not a Rolling Plan.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?

I. Vitamin K is essential for the normal clotting of blood.
II. Scurvy is caused by a deficiency of vitamin D.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. Vitamin K (phylloquinone) is essential for the clotting of blood, since it is required for the synthesis of prothrombin in the liver. Its deficiency causes excessive bleeding and delayed clotting. (विटामिन K — रक्त का थक्का जमना)

 

• Statement II is INCORRECT. Scurvy is caused by a deficiency of VITAMIN C (ascorbic acid), not vitamin D. Its symptoms are bleeding gums, loose teeth and slow healing of wounds.

 

• A deficiency of vitamin D causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vitamins, their chemical names and deficiency diseases:

 

• A – Retinol – night blindness, xerophthalmia

 

• B1 – Thiamine – beriberi; B2 – Riboflavin – ariboflavinosis

 

• B3 – Niacin – pellagra; B12 – Cyanocobalamin – pernicious anaemia

 

• C – Ascorbic acid – scurvy

 

• D – Calciferol – rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults)

 

• E – Tocopherol – sterility; K – Phylloquinone – delayed blood clotting

 

• Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E and K. All the rest are water-soluble, which is why the body cannot store them and they must be taken regularly.

 

NOTE

 

• Since Statement I is correct and Statement II is not, Option 2 (Only II), Option 3 (Both I and II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• The trap in Statement II is a real disease attached to the wrong vitamin. In statement questions of this kind, verify both halves of the pairing separately.

question: In photosynthesis, the oxygen released by green plants is derived from which substance?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Water.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from the splitting of WATER, not from carbon dioxide. (प्रकाश संश्लेषण में मुक्त ऑक्सीजन जल से आती है)

 

• The process is called photolysis of water: under the action of light, water molecules are split into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen —

 

• 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂

 

• This happens in the light reaction, on the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast.

 

• The carbon dioxide taken in is used in the dark reaction (Calvin cycle), in the stroma, where its carbon is fixed into glucose. Its oxygen ends up in the glucose and the water produced, not in the oxygen gas released.

 

• Overall equation: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• This was established by experiments using heavy oxygen (¹⁸O) as a tracer. When plants were given water labelled with ¹⁸O, the released oxygen was labelled; when the carbon dioxide was labelled instead, it was not.

 

• Chlorophyll absorbs light chiefly in the blue and red parts of the spectrum, and reflects green, which is why leaves appear green.

 

NOTE

 

• Carbon dioxide (Option 1): The most tempting answer, since the balanced equation shows six molecules of CO₂ in and six of O₂ out. But the tracer experiments settle the matter — the oxygen released comes from water.

 

• Chlorophyll (Option 2): Chlorophyll is the pigment that traps light energy. It takes part in the reaction but is not consumed and contributes no oxygen.

 

• Glucose (Option 3): Glucose is a product of photosynthesis, not a source of the oxygen gas.

question: Which of the four Vedas is divided into the Shukla (White) and Krishna (Black) recensions?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Yajurveda.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The YAJURVEDA is the only Veda divided into two recensions — the Shukla (White) Yajurveda and the Krishna (Black) Yajurveda. (यजुर्वेद — शुक्ल एवं कृष्ण)

 

• The distinction is one of arrangement, not of doctrine:

 

• Shukla (White) — the sacrificial formulae (*mantras*) are kept separate from the prose explanations, so the text is "clear" or well-ordered. Its Brahmana is the Shatapatha Brahmana.

 

• Krishna (Black) — the mantras and the prose commentary are mixed together, so the text appears unarranged or "dark". Its principal recension is the Taittiriya Samhita.

 

• The Yajurveda is the Veda of sacrificial procedure, telling the priest what to do and say at each step of the ritual. Its priest is the Adhvaryu.

 

• It is the only Veda composed partly in prose as well as in verse.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four Vedas, their priests and their character:

 

• Rigveda – hymns of praise; priest Hotri; the oldest Veda

 

• Yajurveda – sacrificial formulae; priest Adhvaryu

 

• Samaveda – melodies and chants; priest Udgatri

 

• Atharvaveda – charms and remedies; priest Brahma; the last composed

 

• Each Veda has four parts in order: Samhita, Brahmana, Aranyaka and Upanishad — a movement from ritual towards philosophy.

 

NOTE

 

• Rigveda (Option 1): The oldest Veda, a collection of 1,028 hymns in 10 mandalas. It has a single recension in common use, the Shakala.

 

• Samaveda (Option 3): The Veda of melodies, nearly all of whose verses are borrowed from the Rigveda and set to music.

 

• Atharvaveda (Option 4): The Veda of charms, magic and medicine, and the chief source for the popular beliefs of the period.

question:
Which of the following statements regarding Vedic literature is/are correct?

I. The Upanishads are also called Vedanta, meaning the end of the Vedas.
II. The Brahmanas are the portions composed for study in the forest, and deal with the mysticism and symbolism of sacrifice.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. The Upanishads are called VEDANTA, literally *"the end of the Vedas"* — both because they come last in the Vedic corpus and because they represent its culmination in philosophy. (वेदांत — वेदों का अंत)

 

• They deal with Brahman (the universal reality) and Atman (the self), and with the relation between the two. There are 108 Upanishads in the traditional list, of which about 13 are regarded as principal. The motto "Satyameva Jayate" on the national emblem is taken from the Mundaka Upanishad.

 

• Statement II is INCORRECT. The description given belongs to the ARANYAKAS, not the Brahmanas.

 

• ARANYAKAS — from *aranya*, "forest" — were composed for study in the forest by hermits and students who had withdrawn from society, and deal with the mysticism and symbolism of sacrifice.

 

• BRAHMANAS are prose commentaries attached to each Veda, explaining the detailed procedure of the rituals and the meaning of the hymns used in them.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four parts of each Veda, in order:

 

• Samhita – the collection of hymns

 

• Brahmana – prose explanation of the ritual

 

• Aranyaka – the "forest books", on the symbolism of sacrifice

 

• Upanishad – philosophy; the Vedanta

 

• The movement across the four is from ritual to philosophy, and from the household to the forest.

 

NOTE

 

• Since Statement I is correct and Statement II is not, Option 2 (Only II), Option 3 (Both I and II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• Statement II is a correct description attached to the wrong name — the Aranyakas described, the Brahmanas named. This is the commonest form of trap in statement questions.

question: The "Vautha Mela", the annual fair at which donkeys and camels are traded in large numbers, is held in which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gujarat.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Vautha Mela is held at the village of Vautha in the Ahmedabad district of GUJARAT. (वौठा मेला — गुजरात)

 

• It is held on Kartik Purnima, in November, at the confluence of the Sabarmati and the Vatrak rivers — a meeting of waters regarded as sacred, and known as Saptasangam.

 

• It is the only fair in India at which donkeys are traded on a large scale, alongside camels, and thousands of animals change hands during the four or five days it lasts.

 

• The animals are decorated and painted for sale, which gives the fair its distinctive appearance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other well-known fairs of Gujarat: the Tarnetar Mela (a fair at which grooms are chosen, held in Surendranagar), the Bhavnath Mela at Junagadh, the Shamlaji Fair, and the Rann Utsav in Kutch.

 

• Several great fairs of India fall on Kartik Purnima, which makes the date itself worth remembering: Pushkar (Rajasthan), Sonepur (Bihar), Vautha (Gujarat) and Kolayat (Rajasthan).

 

NOTE

 

• Rajasthan (Option 2): The strongest distractor, since Rajasthan holds the far better known Pushkar Fair, a camel fair also on Kartik Purnima — but donkeys are not its business, and Vautha is not in Rajasthan.

 

• Madhya Pradesh (Option 3): Known for the Bhagoria festival of the Bhils and the Malwa Utsav.

 

• Haryana (Option 4): Known for the Surajkund International Crafts Mela, held each February near Faridabad.

question: "Maand", the semi-classical singing style that grew up in the royal courts and is associated with the ballad of Dhola-Maru, belongs to which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajasthan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Maand is a semi-classical singing style of RAJASTHAN, which developed in the royal courts of the region and stands somewhere between folk song and classical music. (मांड — राजस्थान)

 

• Its best-known song is "Kesariya Balam, Aavo Ni Padharo Mhare Desh", which has become the musical signature of Rajasthan.

 

• Its great exponents were Allah Jilai Bai, Gavri Devi and Banno Begum.

 

• The style is closely associated with the romantic ballads of the desert, above all Dhola-Maru.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other song forms of Rajasthan: Panihari (sung by women fetching water), Pabuji ki Phad (a narrative sung before a painted scroll), Panchvani, and the music of the Manganiyar and Langa communities of the western desert.

 

• Rajasthan's instruments: the Ravanahatha (a bowed instrument said to be the ancestor of the violin), the Algoza (twin flutes), the Kamaicha and the Morchang.

 

NOTE

 

• Gujarat (Option 1): Known for Garba, Dandiya Raas and the Duha couplet tradition.

 

• Haryana (Option 2): Known for Ragini and the Saang folk theatre, made famous by Pandit Lakhmi Chand.

 

• Punjab (Option 4): Known for Tappa, Mahiya, Tumbi songs and the Heer ballad, sung to the tale of Heer and Ranjha.

question: The song "Vande Mataram", which became the anthem of the Swadeshi Movement, was taken from which novel?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Anandamath.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Vande Mataram" appears in the novel ANANDAMATH, written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and published in 1882. (वंदे मातरम् — आनंदमठ)

 

• The song itself had been composed earlier, in about 1875, and was later set into the novel, whose subject is the Sanyasi Rebellion of the late eighteenth century.

 

• It was first sung at the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress in 1896, by Rabindranath Tagore, who also set it to music.

 

• During the Swadeshi Movement (1905-08), launched against the Partition of Bengal, it became the movement's rallying cry, and the British authorities prohibited its public singing.

 

• It was adopted as the National Song of India on 24 January 1950 — the same day on which *Jana Gana Mana* was adopted as the National Anthem.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The National Song and the National Anthem are given equal status, though the anthem alone has a prescribed playing time of 52 seconds.

 

• *Vande Mataram* was originally composed in a mixture of Sanskrit and Bengali; the first English translation was made by Sri Aurobindo.

 

NOTE

 

• Durgeshnandini (Option 1): Bankim Chandra's first novel, published in 1865, and generally regarded as the first true novel in Bengali. It is a historical romance set in the Mughal-Pathan wars.

 

• Kapalkundala (Option 3): Another of Bankim Chandra's early romances, published in 1866.

 

• Devi Chaudhurani (Option 4): A later novel by the same author, on a woman who leads a band of rebels — thematically close to *Anandamath*, which makes it the subtlest distractor here.

question: The "Drain of Wealth" theory, which held that India's wealth was being systematically transferred to Britain, was formulated by _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dadabhai Naoroji.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The "Drain of Wealth" theory was formulated by Dadabhai Naoroji, and set out fully in his book "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India" (1901). (धन का निष्कासन — दादाभाई नौरोजी)

 

• The theory held that a substantial part of India's wealth was being transferred to Britain year after year without any equivalent return — through Home Charges, the salaries and pensions of British officials, interest on the public debt, and the profits of British capital.

 

• Naoroji's importance is that he shifted the nationalist argument from grievances about particular policies to an economic critique of colonial rule itself.

 

• He is called the "Grand Old Man of India", was the first Indian to be elected to the British House of Commons (1892, for Central Finsbury), and served three times as President of the Indian National Congress (1886, 1893, 1906).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Naoroji was among the founders of the Indian National Congress in 1885, and it was at the Calcutta session of 1906, which he presided over, that the Congress first declared Swaraj to be its goal.

 

NOTE

 

• R.C. Dutt (Option 1): Author of the two-volume "Economic History of India", which developed and documented the drain theory in detail. He carried the argument forward but did not originate it — which makes him the closest distractor here.

 

• G.K. Gokhale (Option 2): A moderate leader, Gandhi's political mentor, and founder of the Servants of India Society (1905). He was known for his mastery of the budget debates in the Imperial Legislative Council.

 

• M.G. Ranade (Option 3): A pioneer of Indian economic thought and of the Indian school of political economy, who argued for industrialisation as the remedy for poverty. He founded the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha.

question: NavIC, the system developed by ISRO, provides which type of service?
option_1: Weather forecasting over the Indian Ocean
solution_text:
The correct answer is Regional satellite navigation and positioning.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• NavIC stands for NAVigation with Indian Constellation, and it provides regional satellite navigation and positioning services. (नाविक — क्षेत्रीय उपग्रह नौवहन प्रणाली)

 

• Its formal name is IRNSS — the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System. The name *NavIC* was given to it by the Prime Minister, and also means "sailor" or "navigator" in Sanskrit.

 

• Its coverage extends over India and about 1,500 km beyond its borders. It is a regional, not a global, system.

 

• It offers two services: the Standard Positioning Service (SPS) for civilian users, accurate to better than 20 metres, and a Restricted Service (RS) for authorised users.

 

• The constellation consists of seven satellites — three in geostationary orbit and four in geosynchronous orbit.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The global navigation systems of the world:

 

• GPS – United States; GLONASS – Russia

 

• Galileo – European Union; BeiDou – China

 

• NavIC – India (regional); QZSS – Japan (regional)

 

• India's other navigation programme is GAGAN (GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation), developed with the Airports Authority of India to improve accuracy for civil aviation.

 

NOTE

 

• Weather forecasting (Option 1): The work of the INSAT series and of dedicated satellites such as Megha-Tropiques and SCATSAT-1.

 

• Direct-to-home broadcasting (Option 3): The work of the GSAT and INSAT communication satellites.

 

• Earth imaging (Option 4): The work of the IRS, Cartosat and Resourcesat series, used for mapping, resource survey and urban planning.

question: The SI unit of the rate of change of momentum is the same as the SI unit of _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is force.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• By Newton's Second Law of Motion, the rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to the force applied on it, and takes place in the direction of that force. (संवेग परिवर्तन की दर = बल)

 

• F = dp/dt = ma

 

• The SI unit of the rate of change of momentum is therefore the same as that of force — the newton (N).

 

• Checking by dimensions: momentum is kg m/s; its rate of change is kg m/s²; and 1 newton = 1 kg m/s². The two agree exactly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Newton's three laws of motion:

 

• First law – a body continues at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by an external force. This defines inertia, and the law is also called the law of inertia.

 

• Second law – F = ma; force equals the rate of change of momentum.

 

• Third law – to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. This is the basis of the rocket and of the recoil of a gun.

 

• The impulse of a force is F × t, and equals the change in momentum. This is why a cricketer moves his hands back while catching a ball — by increasing the time, he reduces the force.

 

NOTE

 

• energy (Option 1): Measured in joules (J). 1 J = 1 N m — energy is force multiplied by distance, so the units are not the same.

 

• power (Option 2): Measured in watts (W). 1 W = 1 J/s — power is the rate of doing work, not the rate of change of momentum.

 

• pressure (Option 4): Measured in pascals (Pa). 1 Pa = 1 N/m² — pressure is force per unit area, so it differs from force by the area term.

question: "Ganymede", the largest moon in the solar system, orbits which planet?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jupiter.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ganymede is a moon of JUPITER, and is the largest moon in the solar system. (गैनिमीड — बृहस्पति का चंद्रमा)

 

• It is larger than the planet Mercury, though considerably less massive, being composed largely of rock and ice.

 

• It is the only moon known to have a magnetic field of its own, and is believed to hold a subsurface ocean of salt water beneath its icy crust.

 

• Ganymede is one of the four Galilean moons — Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto — discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610 with one of the first telescopes. Their discovery was decisive evidence that not everything in the heavens circled the earth.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Moons worth knowing:

 

• Titan – Saturn's largest; the only moon with a dense atmosphere, and with lakes of liquid methane

 

• Europa – Jupiter; a smooth icy crust over a probable ocean, and a leading candidate in the search for life

 

• Io – Jupiter; the most volcanically active body in the solar system

 

• Triton – Neptune's largest, and remarkable for orbiting backwards

 

• Charon – Pluto's largest, so big relative to Pluto that the two are often called a double system

 

• Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system and has the greatest number of confirmed moons after Saturn. Its Great Red Spot is a storm that has been observed for over three centuries.

 

NOTE

 

• Saturn (Option 1): The strongest distractor, since Saturn's Titan is the second largest moon in the solar system — and larger than Mercury as well.

 

• Uranus (Option 3): Its principal moons are Titania, Oberon, Miranda, Ariel and Umbriel, named after characters in Shakespeare and Pope.

 

• Neptune (Option 4): Its largest moon is Triton, notable for its retrograde orbit, which suggests it was captured rather than formed in place.

question:
In the context of the Union Budget, which of the following is/are capital expenditure?

I. Repayment of loans by the Government
II. Expenditure on the construction of highways
III. Salaries paid to government employees
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Capital expenditure is expenditure that either creates an asset for the government or reduces a liability. Revenue expenditure does neither — it is recurring expenditure on the ordinary running of government. (पूंजीगत व्यय एवं राजस्व व्यय)

 

• Statement I — Repayment of loans: CAPITAL EXPENDITURE. It reduces a liability of the government. Note carefully that the repayment of the principal is capital expenditure, whereas the interest paid on the loan is revenue expenditure.

 

• Statement II — Construction of highways: CAPITAL EXPENDITURE. It creates a durable physical asset.

 

• Statement III — Salaries: REVENUE EXPENDITURE. Salaries are recurring, create no asset and reduce no liability.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four-fold classification of the Budget:

 

• Revenue Receipts – tax revenue and non-tax revenue; neither create a liability nor reduce an asset

 

• Capital Receipts – borrowings, disinvestment, recovery of loans; they either create a liability or reduce an asset

 

• Revenue Expenditure – salaries, pensions, subsidies, interest payments, grants

 

• Capital Expenditure – roads, bridges, machinery, repayment of loans, loans given to states

 

• Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure − Total Receipts excluding borrowings.

 

• Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts.

 

• Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments.

 

NOTE

 

• Only I (Option 1): Correctly identifies the repayment of loans but wrongly excludes highway construction, which plainly creates an asset.

 

• Only II and III (Option 3): Wrongly includes salaries, the clearest example of revenue expenditure in the list.

 

• I, II and III (Option 4): Again wrongly includes salaries. The test to apply to every item is a single question: does it create an asset or reduce a liability?

question: If the nominal Gross Domestic Product of a country rises while its real Gross Domestic Product remains unchanged, what does this imply?
option_1: The volume of production has increased
option_2: The population of the country has fallen
option_3: The general price level has risen
solution_text:
The correct answer is The general price level has risen.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Nominal GDP is measured at current prices; real GDP is measured at the prices of a fixed base year. (नाममात्र जीडीपी एवं वास्तविक जीडीपी)

 

• Because real GDP holds prices constant, it changes only when the volume of output changes. Nominal GDP changes when either output or prices change.

 

• Here real GDP is unchanged, so the volume of production has not changed at all. The rise in nominal GDP must therefore be due entirely to a rise in prices — that is, to inflation.

 

• The relationship is captured by the GDP Deflator:

 

• GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100

 

• If the numerator rises while the denominator stands still, the deflator rises — and the GDP deflator is a measure of the general price level.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The GDP deflator is a broader measure of inflation than the Consumer Price Index (CPI) or the Wholesale Price Index (WPI), because it covers every good and service produced in the economy rather than a fixed basket.

 

• India's monetary policy targets CPI inflation at 4%, with a tolerance band of ±2%, under the framework administered by the Monetary Policy Committee.

 

• The current base year for India's national income estimates is 2011-12.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 is exactly what the figures rule out. Had the volume of production increased, real GDP would have risen — and it has not.

 

• Option 2 brings in population, which affects per capita income but has no bearing on the relation between nominal and real GDP.

 

• Option 4 brings in exports. Exports are one component of GDP, but a rise in them would have raised real GDP as well, which again has not happened.

question: Which of the following plants has been identified in India's national biofuel policy as the principal source of biodiesel?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jatropha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Jatropha curcas has been identified as the principal source of biodiesel in India's biofuel policy. (जट्रोफा — बायोडीजल)

 

• Its seeds contain about 30-40% oil, which is converted into biodiesel by a process called transesterification.

 

• It was chosen for three reasons: it grows on wastelands and degraded soils, it needs very little water, and — crucially — it is non-edible, so its cultivation does not compete with food crops for land.

 

• The National Policy on Biofuels, 2018 sets an indicative target of 5% blending of biodiesel in diesel by 2030, and 20% blending of ethanol in petrol, a target since advanced.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The essential distinction, and the one usually tested:

 

• ETHANOL (blended with petrol) is made from sugar and starch crops — sugarcane molasses, maize, damaged foodgrains.

 

• BIODIESEL (blended with diesel) is made from non-edible oilseeds — jatropha, karanja (pongamia), neem, and also used cooking oil.

 

• Other non-edible oilseeds named in the policy: Pongamia pinnata (karanja), mahua, neem and castor.

 

NOTE

 

• Sunflower (Option 1): An edible oilseed. Its oil can be converted to biodiesel, but using an edible oil for fuel raises the food-versus-fuel objection, which is precisely why the policy avoids it.

 

• Sugarcane (Option 3): The principal source of ETHANOL in India, through molasses and juice — not of biodiesel. This is the strongest distractor, and turns entirely on the ethanol/biodiesel distinction.

 

• Bajra (Option 4): A millet, grown as a food and fodder crop. It is not an oilseed at all.

question: The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana, the crop insurance scheme, was launched in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2016.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) was launched in 2016, and came into operation from the Kharif season of 2016. (प्रधानमंत्री फसल बीमा योजना — 2016)

 

• It is administered by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare.

 

• The premium payable by the farmer is capped at:

 

• 2% of the sum insured for Kharif crops

 

• 1.5% for Rabi crops

 

• 5% for commercial and horticultural crops

 

• The balance of the actuarial premium is shared between the Centre and the State. Since 2020 the scheme has been made voluntary for all farmers, including those with crop loans.

 

• It replaced two earlier schemes — the National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS) and the Modified NAIS.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Major schemes and their launch years:

 

• 2014 – Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana; Make in India

 

• 2015 – Atal Pension Yojana; Jeevan Jyoti Bima; Suraksha Bima; Mudra Yojana; Digital India

 

• 2016 – PMFBY; Ujjwala Yojana; Stand Up India

 

• 2018 – Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY)

 

• 2019 – PM-KISAN, giving Rs 6,000 a year to farmer families in three instalments

 

NOTE

 

• 2014 (Option 1): The year of the Jan Dhan Yojana, the financial inclusion scheme for opening bank accounts.

 

• 2015 (Option 2): A crowded year for schemes — Atal Pension Yojana, Mudra Yojana and the two Bima schemes were all launched in it, which makes it the strongest distractor.

 

• 2018 (Option 4): The year of Ayushman Bharat, the health assurance scheme, and of the National Policy on Biofuels.

question:
Which of the following statements regarding coal in India is/are correct?

I. The Damodar valley is India's most important coalfield region.
II. Most of India's coal reserves are of the anthracite variety.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. The Damodar valley, lying across Jharkhand and West Bengal, is India's most important coalfield region. (दामोदर घाटी — भारत का प्रमुख कोयला क्षेत्र)

 

• Its principal fields are Jharia (the largest, and India's chief source of coking coal), Raniganj (the oldest, worked since 1774), Bokaro, Giridih and Karanpura.

 

• Statement II is INCORRECT. Most of India's coal is BITUMINOUS, not anthracite.

 

• Anthracite is the highest grade of coal, with over 80% carbon, and in India it is found only in small quantities in Jammu & Kashmir.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four grades of coal, in descending order of carbon content:

 

• Anthracite – over 80% carbon; the best quality; burns without smoke

 

• Bituminous – 60-80%; the most widely used, and the type from which coking coal for steel is obtained

 

• Lignite – 40-55%; brown coal; found at Neyveli in Tamil Nadu

 

• Peat – lowest carbon; the first stage of formation

 

• India's coal is of two ages: Gondwana coal, about 250 million years old, which accounts for some 98% of reserves, and the younger Tertiary coal of the north-east.

 

• The largest coal-producing states are Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.

 

NOTE

 

• Since Statement I is correct and Statement II is not, Option 2 (Only II), Option 3 (Both I and II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• Statement II is the standard trap: candidates who know that anthracite is the best grade often assume, wrongly, that it must therefore be the commonest.

question: Who is the author of the Hindi novel "Raag Darbari", a satire on rural politics and administration?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shrilal Shukla.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Raag Darbari" (1968) was written by Shrilal Shukla. (राग दरबारी — श्रीलाल शुक्ल)

 

• It is a satire on the decay of institutions in an Indian village — the college, the cooperative, the panchayat and the local court — set in the fictional village of Shivpalganj in eastern Uttar Pradesh.

 

• Its power lies in its refusal to sentimentalise the village. Where earlier Hindi fiction had treated the countryside as the seat of Indian virtue, *Raag Darbari* shows it as a place where every institution has been captured for private ends.

 

• It won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1970, and Shukla received the Jnanpith Award in 2008 and the Padma Bhushan in 2008.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shrilal Shukla was himself a member of the provincial civil service in Uttar Pradesh, which is the source of the novel's exact knowledge of how the local administration actually works.

 

• *Raag Darbari* was adapted into a television serial for Doordarshan in the 1980s.

 

NOTE

 

• Phanishwar Nath Renu (Option 2): Author of "Maila Anchal" (1954), the great novel of the *Aanchalik* or regional school, set in the Purnea district of Bihar. He also wrote the story "Maare Gaye Gulfam", filmed as *Teesri Kasam*. He is the strongest distractor, since he too wrote of village India — but in sympathy rather than satire.

 

• Nirmal Verma (Option 3): A founder of the Nayi Kahani movement, author of "Ve Din" and "Lal Tin Ki Chhat", and a Jnanpith laureate. His subject is the inner life of the urban and the expatriate.

 

• Yashpal (Option 4): A revolutionary turned novelist, author of "Jhootha Sach", the great Hindi novel of Partition.

question:
Which of the following statements regarding the Indian economy in 1991 is/are correct?

I. India's foreign exchange reserves had fallen to a level sufficient for only about two weeks of imports.
II. The New Economic Policy of 1991 is summarised in the three words Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. By mid-1991 India's foreign exchange reserves had fallen to about one billion dollars — enough to pay for imports for roughly two weeks. The country was on the point of default, and gold was pledged with the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan to raise funds. (विदेशी मुद्रा भंडार का संकट — 1991)

 

• Statement II is CORRECT. The New Economic Policy of 1991 is universally summarised as LPG — Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation.

 

• Liberalisation – abolition of industrial licensing for most industries, easing of controls on trade and investment

 

• Privatisation – disinvestment in public sector undertakings and reduction of the reserved list from 17 industries to 8

 

• Globalisation – integration of the Indian economy with the world through trade and capital flows

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The reforms were introduced by Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh, with an IMF structural adjustment loan.

 

• Immediate measures included the devaluation of the rupee in two steps in July 1991, the New Industrial Policy of 24 July 1991, and the abolition of the MRTP asset limits.

 

• The causes of the crisis were a persistent fiscal deficit through the 1980s, the collapse of the Soviet Union (a major trading partner), and the Gulf War of 1990-91, which raised oil prices sharply and cut remittances from West Asia.

 

NOTE

 

• Since both statements are correct, Option 1 (Only I), Option 2 (Only II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• A figure worth carrying: reserves of about two weeks' imports in 1991, against well over 500 billion dollars today — the contrast is often the point of a question.

question: The city of New Delhi was designed principally by which British architect, working with Herbert Baker?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Edwin Lutyens.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• New Delhi was designed principally by Sir Edwin Lutyens, working with Sir Herbert Baker, after the capital was moved from Calcutta to Delhi at the Delhi Durbar of 1911. (नई दिल्ली — एडविन लुटियंस)

 

• Lutyens designed the Viceroy's House, now the Rashtrapati Bhavan, and laid out the great ceremonial axis of Kingsway, now Kartavya Path (formerly Rajpath).

 

• Baker designed the Secretariat buildings — the North and South Blocks — and the circular Council House, now Sansad Bhavan.

 

• The style is a deliberate blending of classical European architecture with Indian elements — the chhatri, the chhajja and the jaali — and is often called the Indo-Saracenic or Lutyens' Delhi style. The city was formally inaugurated in 1931.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The two architects famously quarrelled over the gradient of the approach to the Viceroy's House. Baker's slope caused the building to sink from view as one climbed towards it — a defeat Lutyens called his "Bakerloo".

 

• Other planned cities of India and their architects: Chandigarh by Le Corbusier (French), Gandhinagar by H.K. Mewada, Bhubaneswar by Otto Koenigsberger, and Jaipur, planned in 1727 by Vidyadhar Bhattacharya for Sawai Jai Singh II.

 

NOTE

 

• Charles Correa (Option 1): A distinguished Indian architect of the modern era, who designed the Gandhi Smarak Sangrahalaya at Sabarmati, the Jawahar Kala Kendra in Jaipur, and planned Navi Mumbai.

 

• Laurie Baker (Option 2): A British-born architect who settled in Kerala and became famous for low-cost, sustainable building in brick. He worked a generation later and in an entirely opposite spirit.

 

• Otto Koenigsberger (Option 4): A German architect and planner who prepared the plan for Bhubaneswar, the new capital of Odisha, in 1948.

question: The agricultural operation by which grain is separated from the harvested stalks is called _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is threshing.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Threshing is the operation by which grain is separated from the stalks and ears of the harvested crop, by beating them or by passing them through a machine. (थ्रेशिंग — गहाई)

 

• It is traditionally done by beating the sheaves against a hard surface, or by driving cattle over them; today it is done by a thresher, and in large farms by a combine harvester, which reaps and threshes in a single operation.

 

• Threshing comes after harvesting and before winnowing.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The sequence of agricultural practices, in order:

 

• Ploughing (tilling) – loosening and turning the soil

 

• Levelling – breaking the clods and making the field even

 

• Sowing – putting the seed into the soil, by hand or by seed drill

 

• Manuring and irrigation

 

• Weeding – removing unwanted plants

 

• Harvesting – cutting the mature crop

 

• Threshing – separating grain from stalks

 

• Winnowing – separating grain from the lighter chaff

 

• Storage – in granaries or silos, after drying

 

NOTE

 

• winnowing (Option 1): The next step after threshing, in which the mixture of grain and chaff is dropped from a height so that the wind carries away the lighter chaff while the heavier grain falls straight down. This is the closest distractor, and the two are constantly confused.

 

• levelling (Option 3): Done before sowing, to break the clods and make the field even so that water spreads uniformly.

 

• sowing (Option 4): The placing of seed in the soil — the beginning of the cycle, not its end.

question: The "Dhad" and "Sarangi", played together by traditional balladeers who sing of local heroes, are associated with which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Punjab.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Dhad and the Sarangi are played together by the Dhadi balladeers of PUNJAB. (ढड्ड एवं सारंगी — पंजाब)

 

• The Dhad is a small hourglass-shaped hand drum, held in one hand and struck with the fingers of the same hand.

 

• A Dhadi jatha is a party of three or four: two or three singers with dhads, and one player of the sarangi, a bowed string instrument.

 

• The tradition is of heroic ballad singing (vaar). It was encouraged by Guru Har Gobind, who employed dhadis to sing of valour and sacrifice before the Sikh congregations, and it remains associated with Sikh history and with the tales of local heroes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other instruments of Punjab: the Tumbi (a single-stringed plucked instrument, made famous by Lal Chand Yamla Jatt), the Algoze, the Chimta, the Dhol and the Ghara (an earthen pot).

 

• The Sarangi, though used here in a folk setting, is also a leading classical instrument of Hindustani music, valued because its sound is held to come closest to the human voice.

 

NOTE

 

• Haryana (Option 1): Its ballad tradition is the Saang folk theatre and the Ragini, accompanied by the Sarangi, Dholak and Nagara. The sarangi is common to both states, which makes this the closest distractor — but the dhad and the dhadi jatha belong to Punjab.

 

• Himachal Pradesh (Option 3): Known for the Ranasingha, the Karnal and the Nagara, played at temple festivals and at the Kullu Dussehra.

 

• Rajasthan (Option 4): Known for the Ravanahatha, the Kamaicha of the Manganiyars, the Algoza and the Morchang.
